Test the three core hypotheses of a hierarchical SDT model

Source: R/hypotheses.R
usdt_hypotheses.Rd

Evaluates the difference between average task sensitivities (H1), their correlation across subjects (H2), and the regression of influence sensitivity on awareness sensitivity (H3). usdt_tests() computes all three together, while individual functions compute them separately.

Usage

usdt_tests(fit, awareness = "d_A", influence = "d_I", level = 0.95)

sensitivity_diff(fit, awareness = "d_A", influence = "d_I", level = 0.95)

latent_cor(fit, awareness = "d_A", influence = "d_I", level = 0.95)

latent_regression(fit, awareness = "d_A", influence = "d_I", level = 0.95)

Arguments

fit

A fitted model: an hsdt object, frequentist or Bayesian, a glmerMod from lme4::glmer() or a brmsfit from brms::brm().

awareness, influence

Character strings naming the sensitivity terms in the model. Defaults match the internal naming of hsdt(). For custom models, both terms must be fixed effects and share a common random-effects grouping by subject.

level

Confidence level for intervals (default is 0.95).

Value

A data frame with columns term, estimate, se, statistic, p.value, conf.low, conf.high, and ci_method. Columns status and reason flag unsupported estimates (e.g., singular fits). usdt_tests() includes an extra hypothesis column (H1, H2, H3).

For a Bayesian hsdt fit the columns are term, estimate (posterior mean), est.error (posterior standard deviation), conf.low and conf.high (central credible interval), ci_method, p.value (two-sided posterior p-value, below 1 - level exactly when the interval excludes zero), rhat and ess_bulk.

Details

These tests run automatically inside hsdt() and appear in its summary. Calling them directly is especially useful when fitting custom models with lme4::glmer() or brms::brm(), allowing you to test these hypotheses while controlling for additional covariates (e.g., set size, experimental groups).

The three hypotheses

  • H1 (Mean difference): Tests whether average sensitivity differs between the awareness and influence tasks.

  • H2 (Correlation): Tests the correlation between task sensitivities across participants using a Fisher-\(z\) transformed interval.

  • H3 (Latent regression): Regresses influence sensitivity onto awareness sensitivity. The intercept represents expected influence performance when awareness sensitivity is zero (\(d'_{\mathrm{Awareness}} = 0\)), testing for unconscious processing.

With positive sensitivity variances, H2 and the H3 slope share the same zero-covariance null. The analytical frequentist output uses the same covariance test for both. The correlation interval uses Fisher-\(z\).

Custom models with covariates

To adjust tests for additional factors, specify the model directly using lme4::glmer() or brms::brm(). As long as the two sensitivity terms are included as fixed effects and correlated across subjects via random slopes, usdt_tests() will compute the latent tests conditional on those covariates. A brms model is summarised from its posterior, like a Bayesian hsdt() fit, and keeps the term names that lme4 would give it. Aggregating the trials with usdt_aggregate() gives either model the same estimates and makes it much faster to fit.

See also

hsdt(), usdt_boot(), usdt_aggregate()

Examples

# 1. Standard model via hsdt()
d <- usdt_data_tasks(
  awareness = vadillo_awareness,
  influence = vadillo_cuing,
  subject_col      = "subj",
  condition_col    = "condition",
  condition_levels = c(signal = "old", noise = "new"),
  response_col     = list(awareness = "judged.old", influence = "rt"),
  response_levels  = list(awareness = c(signal = 1, noise = 0),
                          influence = c(signal = "faster",
                                        noise = "slower")),
  dichotomize      = list(awareness = FALSE, influence = TRUE)
)

m <- hsdt(d)

# All three tests at once
usdt_tests(m)
#>   hypothesis                          term   estimate         se  statistic
#> 1         H1 d'(influence) - d'(awareness) -0.1071347 0.03538288 -3.0278700
#> 2         H2                   correlation  0.4909823 0.51880441  1.0089996
#> 3         H3                     intercept  0.0445278 0.11585861  0.3843288
#> 4         H3                         slope  0.3557591 0.48650940  1.0089996
#>      p.value   conf.low   conf.high ci_method status reason
#> 1 0.00246284 -0.1764839 -0.03778559      Wald     ok   <NA>
#> 2 0.31297483 -0.6654131  0.95424003  Fisher-z     ok   <NA>
#> 3 0.70073479 -0.1825509  0.27160650     delta     ok   <NA>
#> 4 0.31297483 -0.5977818  1.30930002      Wald     ok   <NA>

# Or one test at a time
sensitivity_diff(m)   # H1
#>                            term   estimate         se statistic    p.value
#> 1 d'(influence) - d'(awareness) -0.1071347 0.03538288  -3.02787 0.00246284
#>     conf.low   conf.high ci_method status reason
#> 1 -0.1764839 -0.03778559      Wald     ok   <NA>
latent_cor(m)         # H2
#>          term  estimate        se statistic   p.value   conf.low conf.high
#> 1 correlation 0.4909823 0.5188044     1.009 0.3129748 -0.6654131   0.95424
#>   ci_method status reason
#> 1  Fisher-z     ok   <NA>
latent_regression(m)  # H3
#>        term  estimate        se statistic   p.value   conf.low conf.high
#> 1 intercept 0.0445278 0.1158586 0.3843288 0.7007348 -0.1825509 0.2716065
#> 2     slope 0.3557591 0.4865094 1.0089996 0.3129748 -0.5977818 1.3093000
#>   ci_method status reason
#> 1     delta     ok   <NA>
#> 2      Wald     ok   <NA>

# 2. Custom model with covariates via glmer()
# Controlling for display set size across both tasks
trials <- rbind(
  data.frame(vadillo_awareness[c("subj", "condition", "set.size")],
             task = "A", resp = vadillo_awareness$judged.old),
  data.frame(vadillo_cuing[c("subj", "condition", "set.size")],
             task = "I", resp = meyen_split(vadillo_cuing$rt,
                                            by = vadillo_cuing$subj))
)

# Deviation contrasts (-0.5 vs 0.5). `awareness` flags the awareness task
trials <- within(trials, {
  cond   <- ifelse(condition == "old", 0.5, -0.5)
  size   <- ifelse(set.size == "set size 16", 0.5, -0.5)
  awareness <- as.integer(task == "A")
})

# Counting responses per subject, task and condition keeps the likelihood
# and makes the fit much faster than one row per trial
counts <- usdt_aggregate(trials, response = "resp",
                         by = c("subj", "task", "cond", "size", "awareness"))

# Standard glmer formula: influence criterion is omitted (fixed at 0
# by the median split). Random effects estimate the awareness criterion
# and correlated task sensitivities across subjects.
fit <- lme4::glmer(
  cbind(y, n - y) ~ 0 + awareness + task:size + task:cond +
    (0 + awareness | subj) + (0 + task:cond | subj),
  data = counts, family = binomial("probit"),
  control = lme4::glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa")
)

# Check the names lme4 assigned to the sensitivity terms
names(lme4::fixef(fit))
#> [1] "awareness"  "taskA:size" "taskI:size" "taskA:cond" "taskI:cond"

# Evaluate hypotheses conditional on set size
usdt_tests(fit, awareness = "taskA:cond", influence = "taskI:cond")
#>   hypothesis                          term    estimate         se statistic
#> 1         H1 d'(influence) - d'(awareness) -0.11544746 0.03729771 -3.095297
#> 2         H2                   correlation  0.38184054 0.39474795  0.980489
#> 3         H3                     intercept  0.07364644 0.07325236  1.005380
#> 4         H3                         slope  0.24001573 0.28643288  0.980489
#>       p.value    conf.low  conf.high ci_method status reason
#> 1 0.001966162 -0.18854962 -0.0423453      Wald     ok   <NA>
#> 2 0.326844774 -0.46489654  0.8637596  Fisher-z     ok   <NA>
#> 3 0.314714044 -0.06992556  0.2172184     delta     ok   <NA>
#> 4 0.326844774 -0.32138239  0.8014138      Wald     ok   <NA>

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# 3. The same model fitted with brms. Compiling needs a C++ toolchain
# and the BH and RcppEigen headers for rstan.
fit_b <- brms::brm(
  y | trials(n) ~ 0 + awareness + task:size + task:cond +
    (0 + awareness | subj) + (0 + task:cond | subj),
  data = counts, family = binomial("probit"),
  prior = brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = b),
  chains = 2, cores = 2, seed = 1, refresh = 0
)

# The same term names. The tests now summarise the posterior
usdt_tests(fit_b, awareness = "taskA:cond", influence = "taskI:cond")

# With a proper prior on the sensitivities, also Bayes factors
set.seed(1)
usdt_bf(fit_b, awareness = "taskA:cond", influence = "taskI:cond")
} # }
